Home Insurance Building. The ten-story office building completed in 1885 in Chicago, widely recognized as the world's first steel-frame skyscraper. Though modest in height by modern standards, its revolutionary iron and steel skeleton construction transformed architecture and enabled the vertical city. Designed by architects William Le Baron Jenney, it pioneered the iron skeleton framework that transferred loads to the frame rather than relying on thick load-bearing walls. The use of internal iron supports and external masonry curtain wall created a new structural paradigm, allowing buildings to rise much higher without massive walls at the base. Standing only 138 feet tall at ten stories, it is dwarfed by subsequent towers but represents the crucial invention that made supertall buildings possible. The building's success inspired a generation of Chicago architects, including Louis Sullivan and others, who developed the distinctive Chicago School style. It was demolished in 1931 to make way for the Field Building, erasing the birthplace of modern skyscraper technology. The invention of the steel frame is considered as significant as the development of reinforced concrete and is foundational to modern urban architecture worldwide.
